relationship.direction: natural regeneration of riparian vegetation is constrained where the floodplain soil seed bank has been depleted by prolonged agricultural occupation and where dispersal of desirable species is limited; such sites require active reintroduction of plant material and topsoil remediation rather than passive restoration

context.systems: flooded meadows of Central and Northern Europe; riparian swamps (bottomland hardwood forests) of the Southern U.S.

quote: The paucity of the soil seed bank of the ﬂoodplain after decades of human occupation and limited dispersal of desirable species are widely seen as the main con-straints for the recovery of the plant community in European meadows and U.S. swamps (articles 9, 39, 41, 65 and 139 Appendix S1).

attribution: synthesis of articles 9, 39, 41, 65 and 139 of the review's Appendix S1
selection_justification: This is THE dominant limiting factor of the natural_restored family made explicit: whether a degraded riparian site can regenerate without planting depends on residual seed bank and propagule supply, both degraded by prolonged prior agricultural use. It generalises across two continents and many studies (not n=1 site context), and is a suitability/applicability statement rather than an effectiveness result. VONT GAP flagged: no canonical variable yet exists for regeneration potential in riparian systems (the FMNR analogue `rootstock_presence` is NOT interchangeable - seed bank and living rootstock are different mechanisms), so a descriptive id is used and raised for the team. fined, smaller areas would almost certainly have little
ability to attenuate floods.

relationship.direction: peatland rewetting is targeted where artificial DRAINAGE (canal) DENSITY IS HIGH — peatlands receiving dams averaged 2.5 km km-2, about twice the 1.2 km km-2 of all peatlands; dense canals are what make a peatland both degraded and restorable, so the variable selects the intervention zone rather than excluding it

quote:
Restoration effort was targeted in areas of denser drainage that had experienced high hotspot densities in 2015
(Table 1). The mean canal density of peatlands with dams was 2.5 km km−2, around twice that of all peatlands
(1.2 km km−2) and two‐thirds greater than near wells (1.5 km km−2).

relationship.direction: micro-catchment water harvesting is DEFINED by a runoff-transport distance of less than 100 m from the runoff area to an adjacent infiltration basin — beyond that it is no longer a micro-catchment; the runoff area A and basin B are the two paired elements

quote:
One method of water harvesting is called Micro-Catchment-Water-Har- 
vesting (MCWH), which is defined as collecting surface runoff from a runoff 
area over a distance of less than 100 m and storing it in the rootzone of an 
adjacent infiltration basin to cover the crop water requirement. The runoff 
area A and the area of the infiltration basin B, located downstream of the 
runoff area, are two basic elements of a micro-catchment (Fig. 1 ).
raw_name: defining runoff-transport distance of micro-catchment water harvesting

South, tied ridging was the best followed by mulching practice while in

relationship.direction: runoff/cultivated strips only on flat or gently sloping land

quote: Cultivated strips: On gentle slopes alternating cropping strips along the contour are built: the upper one is used as a catchment and the lower one is cropped. The width of the cropped strip ranges from 1 – 3 m. The C:A ratio is usually 1:1 but can reach 1:5 depending on rainfall and the crop. Often on the sides and the lower end of the cropped area soil bunds are constructed to impede runoff from the cropped area. Cultivated strips are used on flat land or on gentle slopes of up to 4% with at least 1 m deep soils and that receive rainfall of more than 200 mm/y.

relationship.direction: forward-sloping bench terraces extend conservation structures onto steep slopes

relationship.direction: this terrace type is used in semi-arid rainfall
